bull_bear.body:
- Scale leadership in waste-to-energy: JUIL retained its position as India's largest WtE operator with an estimated ~50% share of the country's operational MSW-to-energy processing capacity
- Vertical integration through the Group: in-house access to ductile-iron and MS pipe manufacturing via Jindal SAW supports the water EPC business
- Operating reliability: plants delivered an industry-leading average plant load factor of approximately 90% across the WtE fleet
- Long-tenured contracted revenue: business underpinned by long-tenure government concessions, waste-supply/tipping-fee arrangements and EPC contracts
- Order-book mix quality: a record order book split between EPC (77%) and O&M (23%), giving a recurring, annuity-like cash-flow layer alongside project-driven growth
- Lower cost of capital: upgrade to 'A' Stable by CARE and CRISIL plus closure of Rs 450 crore of NABFID debt for the SIPCOT desalination HAM project, described as a structural improvement in access to long-tenure, lower-cost infrastructure financing
- Off-balance-sheet HAM SPV structure providing annuity cash flows, balance-sheet efficiency and strong risk-adjusted returns
- Parentage: listed holding company for the infrastructure vertical of the O.P. Jindal Group, one of India's largest industrial conglomerates
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Concession, tariff and policy risk — The Group's WtE and water businesses depend on concession agreements, waste-supply and tipping-fee arrangements, and power-purchase agreements with public-sector counterparties; changes in tariff regulation, renewable energy policy or concession frameworks could affect returns. Stated mitigation: robust contractual frameworks, diversified geographic exposure, and proactive engagement with regulators and grantor authorities.
- Receivables and counterparty risk from municipal bodies and discoms — A significant portion of receivables relates to municipal bodies and power distribution companies, whose payment cycles can be affected by procedural approvals and reconciliations. Stated mitigation: strengthened billing discipline, stakeholder engagement and liquidity planning. This is the risk management's own priority list keeps returning to - 'Strengthen collections to improve cash conversion and reduce working-capital intensity' is a named FY27 management priority.
- Project execution and development risk — New WtE and water projects carry construction, commissioning, land acquisition and statutory clearance risks, as well as delays in tariff approvals. Stated mitigation: disciplined project management, phased capital deployment aligned to approvals and financing, and experienced execution teams. Material because roughly half the 220 MW WtE portfolio is still to be commissioned and 11 water projects are targeted for completion in a single year (FY27) against 3 in FY26.
- Financing and interest-rate risk — The capital-intensive project pipeline entails exposure to financing availability and interest-rate movements. Stated mitigation: diversified funding, promoter support, and balance-sheet discipline.
- Commodity and input-cost risk (steel/pipe) — Steel and other input prices affect the water-EPC (pipe) business. Stated mitigation: Group-level integration (in-house pipe and steel access), procurement optimisation and contractual price-adjustment mechanisms where available.
- Feedstock and waste-supply risk — WtE plant economics depend on assured municipal waste supply of adequate calorific value; incomplete source segregation can affect feedstock quality. Stated mitigation: contractual waste-supply assurances and process design suited to Indian MSW.
- Regulatory, environmental and litigation risk — Emissions norms, environmental compliance and contingent liabilities/litigation are inherent to the sector. Stated mitigation: advanced emission-control systems, continuous compliance monitoring and active management of legal matters. No specific case, forum or amount is disclosed anywhere in the routed text.
- Capital intensity and long gestation of the business model — Management characterises the operations themselves as 'capital-intensive, long-gestation and government-facing', which is the framing for the whole risk register; the WtE sector outlook section separately lists 'the capital-intensive nature of projects' and 'long receivable cycles from municipal bodies' as sector risks. [PROVENANCE: the sector risk sentence is in the Corporate Overview/MD&A text delivered to the profile, capex_expansion and registry sibling bundles.]

business.body: The Company operates through a portfolio of subsidiaries and step-down subsidiaries across three reporting segments — Urban Infrastructure, Water Infrastructure and Trading Activities. JITF Urban Infrastructure Limited (JUIL) processes municipal solid waste and generates renewable power through special-purpose vehicles, and is stated to account for close to half of India's operational MSW-to-energy processing capacity; JWIL Infra Limited (JWIL) executes engineering, procurement and construction projects across drinking water, irrigation, wastewater and industrial effluent treatment, and benefits from the Group's in-house access to ductile-iron and MS pipe manufacturing via Jindal SAW. Customers are municipal and urban local bodies, state power distribution counterparties and industrial users, served under long-tenured government concessions and EPC contracts.

business.body:
- **Urban Infrastructure:** Waste-to-energy: municipal solid waste processing and renewable power generation through SPVs, Resource recovery: compost, recyclables and refuse-derived fuel (RDF), Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) certificates generated and sold, Compressed Biogas (CBG) - stated as an adjacent circular-economy opportunity being selectively evaluated, not an existing product
- **Water Infrastructure:** EPC of drinking-water supply schemes, Irrigation projects, Wastewater / sewage treatment projects, Industrial effluent treatment, including operation of a Common Effluent Treatment Plant (CETP), O&M of water assets (annuity-like recurring layer alongside EPC), Desalination under the Hybrid Annuity Model (SIPCOT desalination HAM project)

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: The Group's expansion programme is a waste-to-energy build-out taking a total portfolio of approximately 220 MW from about 110 MW operational in FY2025-26, with the balance expected to be commissioned over the following two years. Six plants are operational - Okhla (20.9 MW) and Tehkhand (25 MW) in Delhi, Jaipur (15 MW, commissioned 20th February 2025) in Rajasthan, Guntur (20 MW, upgraded and operated at 20 MW during the year) and Visakhapatnam (15 MW) in Andhra Pradesh, and Ahmedabad (15 MW) in Gujarat. Four greenfield projects and two brownfield expansions are under way. Jodhpur is a 10 MW greenfield facility held through Jindal Urban Waste Management (Jodhpur) Limited under a 30-year concession with a grant of Rs. 10 Crore; civil work commenced on 10th June 2025 and 70% of work is complete, major packages (TG Set, Boiler, Air-cooled Condenser, Switchyard) have been received at site with installation in progress, and COD is planned on or before October 2026. Bawana is a 36 MW greenfield facility for the National Capital Region under a 25-year concession with a grant of Rs. 151 Crore, described as in an advanced stage of progress having moved swiftly through key regulatory milestones. Kakinada is a 15 MW greenfield facility for the Kakinada-Rajahmundry region of Andhra Pradesh under a 20-year concession with a grant of Rs. 60 Crore. Nellore is a 12 MW greenfield facility for Nellore, Andhra Pradesh under a 20-year concession (the grant figure of Rs. 50 Crore is recoverable only from the risks_esg sibling bundle, where the Directors' Report resumes mid-sentence). Groundwork commenced during FY2025-26 on the Kakinada, Nellore and Bawana projects and on a 17 MW expansion at Okhla; a capacity expansion at Tehkhand is also under way, its size not stated. The Jaipur project comprises a Material Recovery Facility with a design capacity of handling 1000 TPD of MSW, a 15 MW combustion-technology power plant with steam turbine generator, an engineered sanitary landfill and balance of plant, and is designed to recycle all leachate so that the MSW treatment plant operates as a Zero Discharge Unit. On the water side the expansion is order-book and geography led rather than plant led: 11 named projects are targeted for completion in FY2026-27, the SIPCOT desalination HAM project has closed Rs 450 crore of NABFID debt, and the Chambal-Alwar cluster (Rs 6,958 crore across four packages) and Chittorgarh are named as prospective large HAM projects. NO RUPEE CAPEX QUANTUM is disclosed anywhere in the routed text - the only rupee figures attaching to projects are viability-gap grants and concession terms, which are not capital expenditure.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Water scarcity is named as the defining structural driver of demand: India supports close to 18% of the world's population but holds only about 4% of its freshwater resources, and per-capita availability is declining from roughly 1,486 cubic metres in 2021 toward about 1,140 cubic metres by 2050
- Public capital expenditure is the sector's principal demand engine: the Ministry of Jal Shakti was allocated about Rs 99,503 crore in the FY2025-26 Union Budget, channelled through four flagship pillars that 'map directly onto the Company's addressable market'
- Jal Jeevan Mission extended to 2028 as 'JJM 2.0' with emphasis shifting from new connections toward infrastructure quality and long-term O&M of rural piped water schemes - described as 'a meaningful shift in the nature of demand'
- AMRUT 2.0 (indicative outlay about Rs 2.77 lakh crore) targets universal household water-supply coverage across 4,378 statutory towns and 100% sewerage/septage coverage in 500 AMRUT cities, with embedded reforms to meet 20% of water demand through recycled water
- Namami Gange Phase II: commissioned STP capacity reached 3,976 MLD across 173 STPs by Q3 FY2025-26 against a target of 7,000 MLD cumulative sanctioned capacity by December 2026; recent awards use the Hybrid Annuity Model bundling construction with 15 years of O&M
- Used-water management is the single largest structural gap and opportunity: India generates on the order of 72,000 MLD of urban sewage but installed capacity treats only about 37% and actual treatment is roughly 28%
- Industrial demand reinforces the trend, with Zero Liquid Discharge becoming a commercial necessity in water-intensive clusters (textiles at Tiruppur, leather at Kanpur) and coastal desalination emerging as a supplementary source
- Waste-to-energy outlook remains favourable on accelerating urbanisation, rising waste volumes, tightening environmental regulation, the legacy-remediation mandate under SBM 2.0 and India's renewable-energy and net-zero priorities, with installed WtE capacity still far below the MNRE-estimated potential of about 5,690 MW [PROVENANCE: profile/capex/registry sibling bundles - the WtE outlook block is not in this strategy bundle]
- PPP and concession-led delivery: SBM 2.0 encourages private-sector participation and outcome-based funding, and cities are bundling long-tenure concessions with treatment obligations, favouring operators with balance-sheet strength and life-cycle execution capability [PROVENANCE: sibling bundles]
- Expansion beyond metros: rapidly urbanising tier-II cities are emerging as the next wave of demand for advanced waste-processing infrastructure [PROVENANCE: sibling bundles]
- Life-cycle procurement (HAM, DBOT, annuity models) increasingly bundles design, build and 15-plus years of O&M under one structure, rewarding performance over throughput and favouring integrated players [PROVENANCE: profile sibling bundle]
- Operating leverage: with 11 projects slated for completion in FY27 against just 3 in FY26, the Company is described as entering a phase of accelerated revenue recognition as execution converts into billing [PROVENANCE: profile and risks_esg sibling bundles]
- Macro backdrop asserted by management: India GDP growth estimated at 7.4% in FY26 and expected at 6.8-7.2% in FY27, GFCF around 30% of GDP, inflation benign with RBI's FY26 forecast revised to 2.0%
- CAUTION - a generic-boilerplate paragraph in this bundle claims that improving domestic consumption 'underpins volume growth, supports pricing power, and reinforces the long-term consumption fundamentals across its operating categories'; this is a consumer-company template sentence that does not match a municipal-concession/EPC business, and is recorded as stated rather than as a credible driver
- JWIL order book as on 31st March 2026 is INR 11,352 Crores, including an O&M order book of INR 2,585 Crores as on March 31, 2026
- During FY 2025-26, JWIL was awarded orders worth INR 6,922 Crores
- Order book described as up 2.2x year-on-year with a mix of EPC (77%) and O&M (23%), ensuring a recurring, annuity-like cash-flow layer alongside project-driven growth [PROVENANCE: profile sibling bundle]
- EPC order book of Rs 8,767 crores, up 125% from Rs 3,901 crore; O&M order book of Rs 2,585 crores, up 116% from Rs 1,195 crore [PROVENANCE: JWIL 'Key Financial Highlights' block in the profile sibling bundle]
- New order inflow in FY26 comprised 17 new projects [PROVENANCE: profile sibling bundle]
- Completed during FY 2025-26: Nagapattinam, Guwahati C1 and Chhitakhudari projects
- JWIL is planning to complete 11 projects during FY 2026-27: Chidambaram, Nashik, Bhandup, Tanzania, Naini, Ranchi, Sikatia, Palamu, Isarda, Vidisha (Madia Bina Scheme), Parwan
- WtE forward pipeline anchored by six key growth drivers: the Jodhpur, Bawana (greenfield), Kakinada and Nellore Waste-to-Energy projects together with the Okhla and Tehkhand capacity-expansion projects; during FY2025-26 management prioritised execution and development of identified projects over volume-driven order intake [PROVENANCE: profile/capex/registry sibling bundles]
- Chambal-Alwar cluster of Rs 6,958 crore across four packages and Chittorgarh named as prospective large HAM projects, not as booked orders [PROVENANCE: profile and risks_esg sibling bundles]

Achieve commercial operation date of the 10 MW Jodhpur greenfield waste-to-energy facility on or before October 2026; civil work commenced 10th June 2025 and 70% of work is complete, with major packages received at site and installation in progress.
JWIL plans to complete 11 named projects during FY 2026-27: Chidambaram, Nashik, Bhandup, Tanzania, Naini, Ranchi, Sikatia, Palamu, Isarda, Vidisha (Madia Bina Scheme) and Parwan.
Complete 11 water projects in FY27 against just 3 in FY26, converting order book into revenue and cash.

Shift the water order-book mix from Drinking Water to the Integrated vertical (18-25% margin) to drive margin growth over FY27-FY29. [PROVENANCE: profile and risks_esg sibling bundles - not present in this strategy bundle's routed text]
Strengthen collections to improve cash conversion and reduce working-capital intensity, given exposure to municipal and utility counterparties.
Execute the 17 MW Okhla capacity expansion, on which groundwork commenced during FY2025-26, and a capacity expansion at Tehkhand whose size is not stated.

Develop the 12 MW Nellore greenfield waste-to-energy facility in Nellore, Andhra Pradesh under a 20-year concession; the grant of Rs. 50 Crore is stated only in the continuation of this sentence delivered to the risks_esg sibling bundle. No completion date is stated.

Develop the 15 MW Kakinada greenfield waste-to-energy facility for the Kakinada-Rajahmundry region of Andhra Pradesh under a 20-year concession with a grant of Rs. 60 Crore. No completion date is stated.

Construct the 36 MW Bawana greenfield waste-to-energy facility for the National Capital Region under a 25-year concession with a grant of Rs. 151 Crore; the project is in an advanced stage of progress having moved through key regulatory milestones. No completion date is stated.
JWIL is focused on automation and digitalisation of processes along with operational efficiency, and is doing selective bidding for new projects based on parameters laid down by the Board.
Complete expansion projects at Okhla and Tehkhand and greenfield projects at Jodhpur, Bawana, Kakinada and Nellore.

Diversify beyond a single-state focus into industrial water in the NTPC, Mahagenco and SIPCOT zones and new markets in West Bengal, Gujarat (AMC) and Odisha, using the Exim Bank-funded Tanzania project as a base to expand into other African markets.
Selectively evaluate adjacent circular-economy opportunities such as Compressed Biogas (CBG), compost and refuse-derived fuel to broaden revenue beyond power generation.
Expand banking limits, primarily through Non-Fund-Based (NFB / BG) facilities.
Sustain the 'A' Stable rating through disciplined working-capital management and leverage control.
Reuse the SIPCOT HAM financing template (Rs 450 crore from NABFID with no corporate guarantee) for large projects such as the Chambal-Alwar cluster and Chittorgarh.

risks.note: The Group's WtE and water businesses depend on concession agreements, waste-supply and tipping-fee arrangements, and power-purchase agreements with public-sector counterparties; changes in tariff regulation, renewable energy policy or concession frameworks could affect returns. Stated mitigation: robust contractual frameworks, diversified geographic exposure, and proactive engagement with regulators and grantor authorities.

A significant portion of receivables relates to municipal bodies and power distribution companies, whose payment cycles can be affected by procedural approvals and reconciliations. Stated mitigation: strengthened billing discipline, stakeholder engagement and liquidity planning. This is the risk management's own priority list keeps returning to - 'Strengthen collections to improve cash conversion and reduce working-capital intensity' is a named FY27 management priority.
risks.risk: Receivables and counterparty risk from municipal bodies and discoms

risks.note: New WtE and water projects carry construction, commissioning, land acquisition and statutory clearance risks, as well as delays in tariff approvals. Stated mitigation: disciplined project management, phased capital deployment aligned to approvals and financing, and experienced execution teams. Material because roughly half the 220 MW WtE portfolio is still to be commissioned and 11 water projects are targeted for completion in a single year (FY27) against 3 in FY26.
The capital-intensive project pipeline entails exposure to financing availability and interest-rate movements. Stated mitigation: diversified funding, promoter support, and balance-sheet discipline.

Steel and other input prices affect the water-EPC (pipe) business. Stated mitigation: Group-level integration (in-house pipe and steel access), procurement optimisation and contractual price-adjustment mechanisms where available.

WtE plant economics depend on assured municipal waste supply of adequate calorific value; incomplete source segregation can affect feedstock quality. Stated mitigation: contractual waste-supply assurances and process design suited to Indian MSW.

Emissions norms, environmental compliance and contingent liabilities/litigation are inherent to the sector. Stated mitigation: advanced emission-control systems, continuous compliance monitoring and active management of legal matters. No specific case, forum or amount is disclosed anywhere in the routed text.

Management characterises the operations themselves as 'capital-intensive, long-gestation and government-facing', which is the framing for the whole risk register; the WtE sector outlook section separately lists 'the capital-intensive nature of projects' and 'long receivable cycles from municipal bodies' as sector risks. [PROVENANCE: the sector risk sentence is in the Corporate Overview/MD&A text delivered to the profile, capex_expansion and registry sibling bundles.]
